- **Sponsors** (experienced investors) form it; they usually have **a target in mind but do not disclose it**.
- IPO money sits in a **trust account**, may be used **only for the acquisition**, or is **returned on dissolution**.
- After the acquisition the combined company is normally **listed**.
- **Risk:** many SPACs fail; investors can lose money. SPACs compete with **venture capital, private equity, direct listing and the traditional IPO**.
- The courseware states that the **Companies Act, 2013 does not allow blank cheque companies** in India and that a framework was under consideration (position at the courseware date).

**EXIM Bank of India** was set up in **1981** under the **Export Import Bank of India Act, 1981** as the **principal financial institution** for **financing and coordinating the financing of export and import trade**, especially **long-term**. It also arranges **lines of credit to other governments**.

**Its aims**: competitive export finance, new ways of financing, **information and advice** on export openings, selective support for production and marketing, and help with exporters' problems.

**Products**
- **Buyer's Credit**: a **non-LC** facility letting a foreign buyer import Indian goods on **deferred payment**; also **medium and long term** credit to a foreign project company that gives a contract to an Indian project exporter.
- **Corporate banking**: R&D finance, **pre- and post-shipment credit**, import finance, production equipment finance, finance for **SPVs of SME clusters**.
- **Lines of Credit** to overseas **financial institutions, regional development banks and governments** for imports from India on **deferred terms**.
- **Overseas investment finance**: **equity finance** for joint ventures abroad.
- **Project exports**: civil construction, **turnkey**, technical and consultancy services, supplies; **funded and non-funded**.
- **Others**: import loans for third-country projects, merchant banking, **Export Marketing Fund**, **Product Liability Insurance** cost sharing (exports to **OECD** countries), **Export Vendor Development Lending Programme**.

- **Small retail loans**: **by exception or sample**.

**Credit risk** is loss from a counterparty failing. **Market risk** is loss because **prices, interest rates or exchange rates** move so that an asset loses value or a liability rises. The **BIS** definition: the risk that the value of **on- or off-balance sheet positions** is adversely affected by movements in **equity and interest rate markets, currency exchange rates and commodity prices**.

**Components:**

| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Liquidity risk** | **Cash flow gaps** cannot be bridged (for example call money funding a five-year bond that cannot be sold); managed by **knowing due dates** and a **contingency plan** |
| **Interest rate risk** | Rising **funding costs** or falling **asset earnings**; arises from **mismatch** of maturing assets and liabilities |
| **Currency risk** | **Exchange rate moves**; a manifestation of interest rate risk: **interest rate is the domestic cost of currency, exchange rate the external cost** |

**Equity and commodity risks** matter even for limited exposures because they affect **liquidity, interest and exchange rates**. Banks in India may not take commodity exposures except **gold for customers**. Markets are driven by **speculation**, so **perceived future change** matters more than actual change.

A bond pays a **coupon on par value**; it trades at a **premium or discount** to par depending on market interest rates.

- **Yield to maturity (YTM):** the discount rate at which the **present value of all cash flows equals the market price** (NPV at YTM is zero); it assumes **reinvestment at the same rate**.
- **Current yield = coupon / price.** Example: 5 per cent coupon, price 98: **5.10 per cent**.
- **Price and yield move inversely**.
- Two bonds with the same YTM can have **different price sensitivity** (maturity, coupon frequency), so YTM is **not a measure of price volatility**.

The two aims of ALM are **profitability** and **liquidity**. Liquidity, shown by the **quality and marketability** of assets and liabilities, exposes a bank to **liquidity risk**. Unlike other risks it can threaten **solvency** itself: in extreme cases **liquidity problems become solvency problems**.

**Liquidity** = the ability to **accommodate decreases in liabilities** and to **fund increases in assets**. A bank has adequate liquidity when it can get enough funds, **by raising liabilities or converting assets**, **promptly** and **at reasonable cost**.

- The **variability of loan demand and deposits** sets liquidity needs.
- The **price of liquidity** depends on market conditions and perceived **interest rate and credit risk**.
- The market turmoil from **2007** showed the links between **funding liquidity, market liquidity and credit risk**; **Basel III** added the **Liquidity Coverage Ratio** and the **Net Stable Funding Ratio**.

Until about **1970** banks took deposits and lent at **regulated rates**, so rate risk was small. **Deregulation** left pricing to **commercial judgement**; many failures came from **long-term fixed rate assets funded by short-term volatile liabilities**.

**Interest rate risk** = the exposure of a bank's financial condition to **adverse rate movements**. Some risk is a **normal source of profit**, but **excessive risk threatens earnings and capital**.

**Two effects:**

- **Earnings:** rates change **net interest income (NII)** and rate-sensitive fee income and costs.
- **Economic value:** **rising rates raise discount rates and cut market values**; holding **longer-maturity assets than liabilities** means asset values fall **more** than liability values when rates rise.

**NIM = NII / earning assets.** Rate risk arises from assets and liabilities with different **principal amounts, maturity dates or repricing dates**.

The aim is to change the **interest rate sensitivity** of the balance sheet. A cautious bank **matches** assets and liabilities to bring the **gap towards zero**; an aggressive bank **varies the gap with its rate forecast** (expecting rates to rise, it **reprices assets more often than liabilities**).

| To reduce **asset sensitivity** | To reduce **liability sensitivity** |
| --- | --- |
| **Extend investment maturities** | **Shorten investment maturities** |
| **Increase floating rate deposits** | **Increase floating rate lending** |
| **Increase fixed rate lending** | **Increase long-term deposits** |
| **Sell floating rate loans** | **Increase short-term lending** |
| **Increase short-term borrowings** | |
| **Increase long-term lending** | |

**Other options:** match long-term assets with **non-interest-bearing liabilities**; match repriceable assets with repriceable liabilities; use **FRAs, swaps, options and futures** for **synthetic hedges**; keep **NPAs** low because they worsen maturity mismatch. A **full match is neither feasible nor prudent**: set **tolerance limits on gaps**, tighter for the **near buckets**, and build **in-house forecasting skill**.

**Suspension (Section 37):** a bank temporarily unable to pay may apply to the **High Court** to stay proceedings for a **fixed period, total not more than six months**, supported by a **Reserve Bank report** that it will be able to pay.

**Winding up by the High Court (Section 38):** **mandatory** if the bank is **unable to pay its debts** or the **Reserve Bank applies**. It **may apply** if the bank **fails Section 11 capital requirements**, **loses its licence**, is **barred from taking deposits**, a **compromise cannot work**, the **returns show it cannot pay**, or its **continuance prejudices depositors**.

**Deemed inability to pay:** a refused **lawful demand** plus a **Reserve Bank certificate**; the time limit is **two days** where the Reserve Bank has an office or branch, **otherwise five days**. The courts leave the decision to wind up to the Reserve Bank (**Palai Central Bank**).

**Liquidators:** a **court liquidator** attached to each High Court (**Section 38A**); the Reserve Bank, State Bank or another notified bank may be **official liquidator (Section 39)**. The liquidator reports within **two months** and invites claims within **15 days**.

**Voluntary winding up (Section 44):** only if the **Reserve Bank certifies** the bank can **pay all debts in full**.

A **primary co-operative bank** is a society **other than a primary agricultural credit society** that: (i) has **banking as its primary object or principal business**; (ii) has **paid-up share capital and reserves of not less than Rs 1 lakh**; (iii) has **bye-laws that do not admit another co-operative society as a member** (except by subscribing from State Government funds). **Aim:** a **diversified, efficient and competitive** system that improves **allocative efficiency**. **Six groups of reform:** **competition enhancing**, **market forces**, **prudential**, **institutional and legal**, **supervisory** and **technology**.

**Competition enhancing measures:**

- **Operational autonomy** for public sector banks and **raising equity** from the market (**up to 49 per cent of paid-up capital**, as the courseware says).
- **Transparent entry norms** for **private, foreign and joint venture banks and insurers**; **FDI and portfolio investment**.
- **Foreign banks** via **branches**, **wholly owned subsidiary** or a **subsidiary with up to 74 per cent foreign investment** (courseware).
- **New private banks** after **1991** (**HDFC, ICICI, UTI Bank, IDBI**), **differentiated and small finance banks**, **NBFCs**, **core banking migration** and **VRS (2001)**. By **2008** NPAs had fallen from **about 12 per cent** to **just over 2 per cent**.

**Measures enhancing market forces:** **sharp cuts in pre-emption through reserve requirements**; **market-determined pricing of government securities**; **disbanding of administered interest rates**; a **pure inter-bank call money market**; **auction based repos and reverse repos**; **dematerialisation** and **securitisation markets**; and **Targeted Long Term Repo Operations** (banks borrow **on tap** at the **repo rate** for **up to 3 years** for specific sectors).

**Measures enhancing market forces:** **sharp cuts in pre-emption through reserve requirements**; **government securities priced by the market**; **an end to administered interest rates**; a **call money market confined to banks**; **repos and reverse repos by auction**; **dematerialisation** and **securitisation markets**; and **Targeted Long Term Repo Operations** (banks borrow **on tap** at the **repo rate** for **up to 3 years** for specific sectors).

An **organisation** (in the courseware's quotation of Schein) is the rational coordination of the activities of many people to achieve a common, explicit purpose, through **division of labour and function** and a **hierarchy of authority and responsibility**.

- **Formal** organisation: goals, structure, roles and relationships are explicit and documented, to keep decisions consistent.
- **Informal** organisation: roles and relationships evolve from group processes.

Too much structure causes rigidity and slows decisions.

Two streams of thinking developed side by side:

1. how to **organise the activities** most systematically (the work);
2. how to understand the **individual's relation to work** (the person).

Early figures: **Robert Owen** (workers are "vital machines", so better conditions raise productivity) and **Charles Babbage** (division of labour, scientific principles of work).

An **attitude** is a **persistent tendency to feel and behave in a particular way** towards some object: a person, a bank, a product, a practice, an idea.

Three features: it **persists** unless something changes it; it lies on a **continuum** from very favourable to very unfavourable; and it is **directed at an object** about which the person has perceptions, feelings and beliefs, which can make opinions emotionally charged.

Attitudes are **not** built on complete, objective information, which is why two people can hold different attitudes to the same thing.

| Component | Content | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Emotional** | Feelings: positive, neutral or negative | "I dislike touring" |
| **Informational** | Beliefs and information, perhaps inaccurate | A manager believes two weeks of training is enough when four are needed |
| **Behavioural** | The tendency to act | The manager allows only two weeks |

**Career planning** is systematically matching career goals and individual capabilities with opportunities. In a bank it is an HRD subsystem linking manpower planning, job rotation, transfer, placement, training and appraisal. It structures employees' **aspirations** for upward movement and **moderates unrealistic ones**. It does **not** commit management to promote anyone: the path is a **facility for growth, not a right**.

**What the organisation should do:** state the policy and benchmarks; encourage growth and discourage superiors who suppress it; make the path **known from entry**, with performance feedback; apply it **without bias**; keep it **flexible**.

**Four steps to chalk out the path:**

1. **Define the career stages** (apprentice, colleague, mentor, sponsor) against organisational levels.

Herzberg asked about 200 accountants and engineers when they felt exceptionally good and exceptionally bad about their jobs (the critical incident method). Good feelings came from the **job content**; bad feelings from the **job context**. So the two sets are separate:

| | **Motivators (satisfiers)** | **Hygiene (maintenance) factors** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relate to | The **job itself** (content) | The **surroundings** (context) |
| If present | Create a strongly motivating situation | Do **not** significantly motivate |
| If absent | No dissatisfaction, only no motivation | **Serious dissatisfaction**, lower performance |
| Items | Recognition, advancement, responsibility, achievement, possibility of growth, work itself (6) | Company policy and administration, technical supervision, relations with subordinates, salary, job security, personal life, working conditions, status, relations with supervisors, relations with peers (10) |

**Counselling** means advising the employee about performance. It comes **after** the appraisal interview and feedback, when the superior concludes that performance is **far below** expected and needs **immediate, major** corrective action. It is defined as using a set of skills to help another person take **responsibility** for and manage his own work-related decisions.

- Offer **workable solutions** and act where the appraisee can start to improve.
- Avoid **prejudice**; weigh the employee's version objectively.
- **Successful counselling is effective listening.**

Clear key result areas lower the chance of falling short through **ambiguity**.

old:
**BEI** is a **structured interview** that collects information about **past behaviour**, on the premise that the **best predictor of future behaviour is past behaviour**. It asks open-ended questions in which the interviewee describes in detail past experiences that show how he performed. It is the heart of the **job competency assessment** process and its data are the richest source of competency data. **Principle:** what people *say* about their motives and skills is not credible; only what they *actually did* is, so the interviewer gets people to describe how they **behaved in specific incidents**.

**Five steps:**

1. **Introduction and explanation**: build trust and goodwill; put the interviewee at ease.
2. **Job description**: most important tasks, responsibilities, desired output.
3. **Behavioural events** (the bulk of the time): complete stories of critical incidents, gathered with the **STAR** technique: **S**ituation, **T**ask, **A**ction, **R**esult.
4. **Characteristics needed to do the job**: knowledge, skills, abilities the interviewee thinks are needed.
5. **Conclusion and summary**: thank, ask what may have been overlooked, and summarise in a set format.

**Limitations:** it depends on the **respondent's recall** (only what is remembered or chosen is given, possibly self-serving); it gets at actions, thoughts and feelings but not the **knowledge** behind them, so it is a weak source of **specialised knowledge**; and interpretation depends on the **interviewer**, who may not be an expert, leaving room for guesswork.

**BEI** is a **structured interview** that collects information about **past behaviour**, on the footing that **what people did before is the best guide to what they will do**. It asks open-ended questions in which the interviewee describes in detail past experiences that show how he performed. The **job competency assessment** process is built around it, and no other source yields richer competency data. **Principle:** people's own account of their motives and skills cannot be relied on; what they *actually did* can, so the interviewer gets people to describe how they **behaved in specific incidents**.

**Five steps:**

1. **Introduction and explanation**: build trust and goodwill; put the interviewee at ease.
2. **Job description**: most important tasks, responsibilities, desired output.
3. **Behavioural events** (the bulk of the time): complete stories of critical incidents, gathered with the **STAR** technique: **S**ituation, **T**ask, **A**ction, **R**esult.
4. **Characteristics needed to do the job**: knowledge, skills, abilities the interviewee thinks are needed.
5. **Conclusion and summary**: thank, ask what may have been overlooked, and summarise in a set format.

**Limitations:** it depends on the **respondent's recall** (only what is remembered or chosen is given, possibly self-serving); it gets at actions, thoughts and feelings but not the **knowledge** behind them, so it is a weak source of **specialised knowledge**; and interpretation rests with the **interviewer**, who is not always an expert, which leaves room for guesswork.

**Conflict** is a sharp disagreement or opposition of interests or ideas. It arises whenever people have different **values, opinions, needs and interests** and cannot find a middle way. The courseware defines it as a clash between individuals arising from differences in **thought process, attitudes, understanding, interests, requirements and even perceptions** (McLean: the struggle associated with the perception of opposing goals, desires, demands, wants or needs).

It shows as insults, non-cooperation, bullying and anger. Causes run from **personality clashes** to **misunderstood communication** to **organisational mismanagement**. Costs: disrupted work, lower productivity, absenteeism, turnover, even termination; stress can be both a cause and an effect.

**Banks and conflict:** because banks are **custodians of public money**, the courseware says conflict management should be assigned to executives with the right skill and strategy, and an executive's handling of conflict should appear among **key performance indicators** in appraisal. The employer's main tool is a **culture of fairness, trust and mutual respect**.

Key point: conflict is a **normal** part of any relationship. The aim is not to fear or avoid it but to **resolve it in a healthy way**; how it is handled can strengthen or destroy a relationship.

**Intra-individual** (intra-personal) conflict arises when a person's objectives differ from the company's vision, from frustration, from roles that demand equal attention, and from goals with positive and negative features.

**Goal conflict** (attaining one goal excludes another):

| Form | Choice between |
| --- | --- |
| **Approach-approach** | Two or more **positive**, mutually exclusive goals |
| **Approach-avoidance** | A single goal with **both** positive and negative features |
| **Avoidance-avoidance** | Two or more **negative**, mutually exclusive goals |

**Frustration:** a motivated drive is **blocked** before the goal is reached, by external barriers (non-social such as power failures or transport breakdown; or social) or internal ones (limitations, lack of skill; more lasting). Four defences: **aggression** (attack the barrier), **withdrawal** (back away), **fixation** (keep trying to break through), **compromise** (find a new goal).

**Role conflict:** playing several roles at once with too little time or resources.

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Person-role** | Between the person's personality and the role's expectations |
| **Intra-role** | Contradictory expectations about how **one** role should be played |
| **Inter-role** | Differing requirements of **two or more** roles played at the same time |

The courseware's easiest formula: **Listen, Talk, Resolve**. | Approach | Meaning | Assertiveness / cooperativeness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Avoiding** | Ignore or sidestep the conflict | Low / low |
| **Accommodating** | Satisfy the other's concerns at your own expense | Low / high |
| **Competing** | Satisfy your desires at the others' expense | High / low |
| **Collaborating** | A solution that fully satisfies all parties | High / high |
| **Compromising** | A partial satisfaction for all | Medium / medium |

In most conflicts **neither party is simply right**: different perceptions collide. Conflict management aims at **minimising affective conflict** (about feelings and relationships) at all levels and keeping a **moderate amount of substantive conflict** (about the work).

**Styles** the courseware names:

| Author | Styles |
| --- | --- |
| **Follett** | Domination, compromise, **integration** (open exchange to find a solution acceptable to both) |
| **Blake and Mouton** | Forcing, withdrawing, smoothing, compromising, problem solving |

No style fits every situation.

**Do not** avoid a conflict hoping it will go away. Ask participants to describe the **specific actions** they want from the other party; consider a **third party** (a non-direct superior with access to the situation).

**Preventive actions:** regular review of **job descriptions**; **rapport** with subordinates; regular **reports**; **training** in communication, conflict management and delegation; **mutual development of procedures**; regular **meetings**; a **suggestion box**.

**Policy elements:** acknowledge the problem; let people express feelings; define the problem; find the **underlying need**; find **common ground**, however small; find solutions that satisfy needs (silence may be passive resistance); **follow up**; and if unresolved, use an **outside facilitator** or treat it as a **performance issue**.

**ICT** (information and communication technologies) is the umbrella for technologies combined with the internet, social media, mobile communication and computers. Its effect on HR is mainly in **how information is collected, stored, used and disseminated**. Benefits: lower administrative expense, higher productivity, better decisions and customer service.

The courseware's observations on why HR needs a database:

1. Many functionaries inside and outside HR use the **same basic employee information**: a **shared database** avoids duplicate collection.
2. The employee record is **broad-based** (experience, training, competencies, skills, performance, expectations, as well as pay, leave and increments), so it is large.
3. Different people can **update parts** from different locations.
4. Decisions should be **embedded in the data** for objectivity and consistency (for example choosing the right person for a training).
5. **Policy review** needs analysis of whether practices work and whether there is **bias**.
6. **Statutory requirements** call for such a database.

The answer: a computer-based **HRIS**, with security measures for **confidentiality, integrity, availability and access control**. The aim of automation is to help managers work faster and focus on managing the workforce.

**Knowledge management (KM)** is the process of **creating, identifying, storing, distributing and pooling** an organisation's knowledge and structuring it for effective use; in particular, **capturing the tacit knowledge** of people for future use. Knowledge workers must be continually **re-skilled**. In banks the issue is sharpened by competent employees leaving for other banks. An organisation using KM as strategy must first **identify its knowledge workers** (creators, handlers, processors).

**Five core components to assess:**

| Component | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **People** | Individuals' ability to influence others with their knowledge |
| **Processes** | Best practices and governance for identifying, managing and sharing knowledge |
| **Technology** | Tools and automation that enable KM |
| **Structure** | Organisation that encourages cross-discipline awareness |
| **Culture** | A knowledge-sharing, knowledge-driven culture |

**Eight implementation steps:** 1 establish objectives; 2 prepare for **change** (KM is a culture change: rewarding only individual performance breeds "knowledge is power"); 3 define a high-level process; 4 define technology needs; 5 assess present KM status; 6 draw an implementation plan; 7 implement (celebrate short-term wins); 8 **monitor and measure** (baseline and balanced scorecard).

**Benefits (courseware):** lower costs; improved decision-making; easy to find information; tracking ideas and documents; **preventing brain drain**; **learning from mistakes**; faster delivery to clients; growth and innovation; standardised processes; better service to employees and customers.

Compare **two balance sheets**. Each change in an item (other than cash) is a **source** or a **use** of funds:

| Change | Source or use |
| --- | --- |
| **Increase** in a **liability** | **Source** |
| **Decrease** in an **asset** | **Source** |
| **Increase** in an **asset** | **Use** |
| **Decrease** in a **liability** | **Use** |

The statement shows what happened to the excess of **long term sources over long term uses**, that is, to **net working capital**. If **more is used long term than raised long term**, net working capital **falls**: the funds have been **diverted** (for example, short term money financing long term assets).

A **related party transaction** is a **transfer of resources, services or obligations** between a reporting entity and a related party, **whether or not a price is charged** (Ind AS 24, as the courseware quotes it).

**A person (or close family member) is related if they:** have **control or joint control**, have **significant influence**, or are **key management personnel** of the entity or its parent.

**An entity is related if it is:** in the **same group**; an **associate or joint venture** of the other; **joint ventures** of the same third party; a **post-employment benefit plan** for either entity's employees; or **controlled or significantly influenced** by an identified person.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Control** | Power to govern **financial and operating policies** to get benefits |
| **Joint control** | **Contractually agreed** sharing of control |
| **Key management personnel** | Those with **authority and responsibility** for planning, directing and controlling |
| **Significant influence** | Power to **participate** in policy decisions **without control** |

**Raising a concern:** in **writing or verbally** to the **ombudsperson or CVO** (a verbal complaint is **written up** by the ombudsperson). The ombudsperson, CVO or **audit committee** checks whether a breach occurred and **responds within 2 days** of receiving the complaint.

**Identity:** the whistle-blower may or may not reveal it; either way the complaint is **taken seriously**, and the **identity is kept confidential** in all cases. **False allegations** bring **strict disciplinary action**.

**Investigation:** the committee **contacts** the employee, vendor or stakeholder, decides **internal steps**, keeps everything **confidential** and **shares status and findings with the Board**, with a **final report** holding all details and documents.

**Alternative routes:** manager or **head of department**, **HR**, **legal**, **Compliance Head**, **CEO or CVO**, **management committee members**; in an **urgent** case **write directly to the chair of the audit committee**; a complaint received by HR goes to the **director of human resources**.

**Four components of a policy:** a **whistle-blower**, a **wrongful or unethical practice** (grave and serious, not trivial), an **authority** (independent, senior, responsible; a defined escalation process) and **a policy** (with **direct access to the chair of the audit committee**).

**Five reasons staff do not report (ACFE):** **no corrective action**, **no confidentiality**, **retaliation by superiors**, **retaliation by co-workers**, **unsure whom to contact**.

**Definition:** transparency is the **absence of asymmetric information** between policy makers and other agents, **reducing uncertainty**. It is needed because of **financial crises caused by information gaps**, **integrated markets**, **greater autonomy and accountability** and the **stress on financial stability**. It is a **secondary but important objective**: the bank is an **agent** answerable to the public (**principal-agent** relationship). **Disclosure** deters **discretionary policy**, **time inconsistency** and **excess risk taking**, and makes **policy more effective** if the public **understands the goals and instruments**.

**International initiatives:** began at the **1995 Halifax Summit (G-7)**; after the **East Asian crisis**, in **April 1998** finance ministers and central bank Governors set up **three working groups**: **transparency and accountability**, **strengthening domestic financial systems**, **managing international financial crisis**.

**IMF Code of Good Practices on Transparency in Monetary and Financial Policies (March 2000)** and the **ELRIC** framework (**E**xternal audit mechanism, **L**egal structure and independence, financial **R**eporting, **I**nternal audit mechanism and a system of internal **C**ontrol); the IMF **safeguards assessment** is a **diagnostic** of these five areas.

**Twelve key standards (after the 1994 Mexican crisis, Task Force chaired by Andrew Sheng):**

| Area | Standard | Body |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monetary and financial policy transparency | **Code of Good Practices** | **IMF** |
| Fiscal transparency | **Code of Good Practices on Fiscal Transparency** | **IMF** |
| Data dissemination | **SDDS / GDDS** | **IMF** |
| Insolvency | **Principles and Guidelines on Effective Insolvency and Creditor Rights System** | **World Bank** |
| Corporate governance | **Principles of Corporate Governance** | **OECD** |
| Accounting | **International Accounting Standards** | **IASB** |
| Auditing | **International Standards on Auditing** | **IFAC** |
| Payment and settlement | **Core Principles for Systemically Important Payment Systems** | **CPSS-BIS** |
| Market integrity | **Forty Recommendations (money laundering)** | **FATF-OECD** |
| Banking supervision | **Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision** | **BCBS** |
| Insurance supervision | **Insurance Core Principles** | **IAIS** |

**Credibility** is an **intangible asset**, hard to measure, but shown by a **track record** of achieving **price stability**.

**Rangarajan High-Level Committee on Balance of Payments (1993):** a **market-determined exchange rate within limits**; **current account convertibility**; **shift from debt to non-debt flows**; **strict regulation of external commercial borrowings (short-term debt)**; **discourage volatile NRI flows**; **free outflows tied to inflows** and gradual freedom for others; **end Government intermediation of external assistance**.

**Milestones:** **LERMS** (dual rate) **March 1992**; **unified market rate from March 1993**; **Article VIII of the IMF Articles accepted in August 1994** (current account convertibility); **Sodhani Expert Group** (**November 1994**, report **June 1995**) on the forex market; **Tarapore Committee on Capital Account Convertibility (1997)**, which set **three preconditions**: **fiscal consolidation**, a **mandated inflation target** and **strengthening the financial system**.

**FEMA, 1999 (effective June 2000)** replaced **FERA, 1973**: from **conservation** to **management** of foreign exchange; **genuine current account payments** (except notified items) are released by **authorised dealers** without restriction; **surrender of export proceeds** continues; the RBI controls **capital account transactions**.

**Differences from FERA (Box 5.1):** **civil**, not criminal, treatment: the prosecution **need not prove guilt**; **monetary penalties**; an **Adjudicating Authority, Special Director (Appeals) and Appellate Tribunal**; **compounding**: a contravener may apply, and the **compounding authority must decide within 180 days**; the **Reserve Bank** is the compounding authority for all contraventions **except hawala**, where the **Directorate of Enforcement** is.

**Market development:** wide delegation to **authorised dealers**; **options, cross-currency options, swaps, caps/collars and FRAs**.

**What it is:** a **cost-free redress** mechanism for **deficiency in service** by **regulated entities**, under **Section 35A (BR Act)**, **Section 45L (RBI Act)** and **Section 18 (PSS Act)**. It **integrates** the **Banking Ombudsman Scheme 2006**, the **NBFC Ombudsman Scheme 2018** and the **Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions 2019** (**all repealed**); it also covers **non-scheduled primary co-operative banks with deposits of Rs 50 crore and above**; **One Nation One Ombudsman** (**jurisdiction neutral**).

**Features:** the complainant **need not name the scheme**; **deficiency in service** is the ground with a list of **exclusions**; **no territorial jurisdiction per office**; a **Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre, Chandigarh**; the regulated entity's **Principal Nodal Officer** is a **General Manager** (or equivalent) at **head office**; the **Appellate Authority** is the **Executive Director in charge of the Consumer Education and Protection Department**; an entity **cannot appeal** an Award issued because it **did not give satisfactory information on time**.

**Awards:** no cap on the **amount in dispute**; compensation for **consequential loss up to Rs 20 lakh** plus **up to Rs 1 lakh** for **time, expenses, harassment and mental anguish** (courseware, dated). The Ombudsman is an **RBI officer** appointed for **up to three years**; an **annual report** goes to the **Deputy Governor** as on **31 March**.

**Complaint is not maintainable** for: **commercial judgment** of the entity; **vendor outsourcing disputes**; a grievance **not addressed to the Ombudsman directly**; **general grievances against management**; **action under orders of a statutory or law enforcing authority**; services **outside RBI purview**; disputes **between regulated entities**; **employer-employee disputes**; a remedy under **Section 18 of the CIC Act**; customers not covered.

**A complaint lies only if:** the complainant first **complained in writing to the entity** and the reply was **rejected or unsatisfactory** or **no reply came in 30 days**; the complaint reaches the Ombudsman **within one year** of the reply (or **one year and 30 days** from the complaint if no reply); it is **not pending or decided elsewhere** (Ombudsman, court, tribunal, arbitrator); **not frivolous or abusive**; the first complaint was within **Limitation Act** time; the complainant gives **complete information**; and it is lodged **personally or by an authorised representative who is not an advocate**.

**Procedure:** file **online (cms.rbi.org.in)** or via the **Centralised Centre**; the entity files its **written version within 15 days**; failing which the Ombudsman may pass an **ex-parte order**. **Resolution:** **settlement**, **complainant's agreement** or **withdrawal**. An **Award** **lapses unless accepted in 30 days** and the entity **complies within 30 days of acceptance** unless it appeals. **Appeals:** the **entity** (with **prior sanction of the CMD/CEO or ED**) or the **complainant** within **30 days** (up to **30 more** on cause); the **Appellate Authority** may **dismiss, allow, remand, modify** or pass other orders. Banks must **display** the **Ombudsman's contact details** and the **Scheme**, appoint **Nodal Officers** at regional and zonal offices and a **Principal Nodal Officer**.

**Four approaches to supervision:**

| Approach | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Institutional** | Each **category of institution** has its own supervisor (traditional) |
| **By objectives** | Each authority handles **one objective** (for example **prudential** or **conduct**) across institutions |
| **Functional** | Supervision follows the **economic function**, whatever the institution |
| **Single regulator** | **One authority** for **all markets and intermediaries** (the **UK FSA** model) |

No model is clearly superior; **most countries** keep **bank supervision in the central bank**.

**India (institutional model):** the **Reserve Bank** supervises **banks, NBFCs and all-India financial institutions**; the **Registrar of Co-operatives (State)** is a **joint regulator** of **co-operative banks**; **SEBI** regulates **capital markets** (stock exchanges, mutual funds, brokers, merchant bankers, rating agencies); **IRDA** regulates **insurance**.

**Overlap and coordination:** the **Khan Working Group** argued for a **Super Regulator** and the **Deepak Parekh Group** for **legal status** for the **High Level Coordination Committee on Financial and Capital Markets (HLCC)**, chaired by the **Governor** with the **Finance Secretary** and the **Chairmen of SEBI and IRDA**, with **three Technical Standing Committees** (banking, insurance, capital markets). Other views: the **duality of control** between the Reserve Bank and the **Banking Division, Ministry of Finance** should end; an **apex regulatory authority** chaired by the **Governor** could coordinate. The courseware concludes that **regulatory overlaps and arbitrage are small** and that the Indian model works with **coordination**.

**Meaning:** monetary policy changes the **supply of money** to promote **growth with price stability**. Money is a **liability of the Government and the central bank** and an **asset of the public**, so policy changes **portfolio choices**.

**Typical goals:** **maximum feasible output**, **high growth**, **full employment**, **price stability**, **fairer distribution** and a **healthy balance of payments**.

**The chain:** **Instruments → Indicators → Targets → Goals**. The further from the instrument, the **harder it is to measure** the effect. **Target variables** should be **close to goals**, **quickly influenced by policy** and **observable**: **money supply, bank credit, interest rates**. **Money supply** is preferred because policy factors dominate it. An **indicator** should show the **intensity of policy**: of the four (**high powered money, money supply, bank credit, interest rates**), **high powered (reserve) money** is the better indicator since the **money multiplier is behavioural**. Example: a **CRR change** alters **reserve money**, then **money supply**, then **prices**.

**Tinbergen principle:** **n objectives need at least n instruments**.

**Price stability argument:** it gives investors a **stable climate**, protects **poorer sections**, and avoids **redistribution between creditors and debtors**. **Barro**: **inflation above about 10 per cent hurts growth**, **optimal growth** needs inflation **below about 7 per cent**; a recent study puts the **threshold at 1-3 per cent for industrial** and **7-11 per cent for developing** countries; the courseware reports that **4 per cent (± 2 per cent)** is the **comfort zone** for the Reserve Bank.

**Single inflation target:** **transparent, clear, holds the bank accountable**; given as a **band**. Some countries (**New Zealand, Canada, UK, Australia, Sweden, Finland, Spain**) adopt **price stability as the sole objective**; the **US** follows a **dual mandate**.

**Reconciling dual objectives:** **unemployment data are weak**, so banks estimate **potential output** and try to **minimise the output gap** (actual vs potential output); in developing economies the **trend growth** is used as a proxy.

**Credit policy** is the policy of the central bank on **the cost and availability of bank credit** to the sectors of the economy; it is a **sub-theme (adjunct) of monetary policy** with a **two-fold role**: its effect on **investment and growth** and on **money supply** (credit creation adds money).

**Dimensions:** the **quantum**, **sources** (institutional and non-institutional; banks are the main source), **nature of requirements** and **allocation mechanisms**.

**Differences from monetary policy:** money is an **asset of the public but a liability of the Government and the central bank**; **bank credit is an asset of banks and a liability of the public**. In a developing country it is not enough to decide the **total credit**: it must also be **allocated across sectors, regions and groups** (sectoral, regional and equity concerns). Instruments are mostly the **same**; credit policy is administered by the central bank.

**What the Reserve Bank regulates:** the **cost**, the **quantity** and the **purpose** of credit; **productive** needs of **agriculture, trade and industry**, **not speculative** uses.

**In practice:** the bank considers the **market borrowing programme**, **foreign capital flows** and **deposit mobilisation** to set the desired **credit expansion**, which also shows the split between **Government** and **commercial sector**. Credit is then allocated **by activity** (agriculture, manufacturing, trade), **by industry class**, **to priority sectors**, and **by region (rural vs urban)**. The **credit budget** is an **offshoot of the monetary budget**; credit planning also means building **infrastructure and channels** for delivery.

The Centre chose **gradual consolidation** (a **GFD of 6.8 per cent of GDP in 2021-22**, from **9.4 per cent**, falling to **below 4.5 per cent by 2025-26**), emphasising **capital expenditure** (**2.5 per cent of GDP** vs an average **1.7 per cent** in 2010-20).

**Support to States (2020-21):** the **WMA limit raised by 60 per cent (April 2020)**, extended by **Advisory Committee on WMA to State Governments (2021)**; **overdraft days** increased; looser rules on **withdrawing from the Consolidated Sinking Fund**; **interest-free 50-year loans** for **capital expenditure**; **net market borrowing of up to 4 per cent of GSDP in 2021-22** (more with **power sector reforms**).

**Three areas:** **tax devolution**, **grants** and **fiscal roadmap/rules**.

**Tax devolution:** **FC-11** widened the **shareable base to all Union taxes** (excluding **cesses and surcharges**); **FC-14** sharply raised the **devolution ratio** after the **Planning Commission was abolished** and **plan grants ended**. Growth in cesses and surcharges (**outside the divisible pool**) reduced the benefit. **FC-15** kept the **ratio** (adjusted for **Jammu and Kashmir**) for **stability**. **Horizontal sharing** (among States) has used **equity criteria since FC-8**; **FC-15** moved the **population base from 1971 to 2011**, added a **demographic performance** criterion (**to reward population control**: the **inverse of the 2011 total fertility rate times the 1971 population**) and **brought back the tax effort** criterion (used by FC-10 to FC-12, dropped by FC-13 and FC-14).

The **FRBM Act, 2003** sets targets for **fiscal discipline**.

**Roadmap (dated):** Union GFD from **9.3 to 6.8 per cent of GDP (2021-22 to 2025-26)**, **debt 89.6 per cent peak** and **85.7 per cent by 2025-26**; States' GFD from **6 to 4 per cent of GSDP**, debt **62.9 to 56.6 per cent**; an **inter-departmental group** to review **FRBM**.

**Patel Committee (2014):** avoid **reliance on overnight variable rate repos**; **term repos of different tenors** provide the **bulk of liquidity**; **end unlimited accommodation at the fixed repo rate**; **fine-tuning repos/reverse repos** (**overnight to 28 days**); **phase out export credit refinance**.

**Internal Working Group (IWG, constituted 6 June 2019, report 26 September 2019):**

- **Corridor** (not floor) system continues.
- **WACR** remains the **operating target**.
- Desired system liquidity: a **small deficit of about 0.25 to 0.5 per cent of NDTL**; use **variable rate operations** if surplus arises.
- **Day-to-day:** one **overnight variable rate operation** at a rate **close to the repo rate**; **no separate assured liquidity**; **standalone primary dealers** may take part directly; **intra-day fine-tuning** only for **unforeseen shocks**.
- **Durable liquidity:** build-ups beyond **0.25 to 0.5 per cent of NDTL** should be offset by **OMOs, forex swaps** and **longer-term (above 14 days up to one year) variable rate repos and reverse repos**.
- **Corridor edges:** **25 bps** between **repo and reverse repo** and between **repo and MSF** retained; **margins** reviewed (reverse repo margin **nil**); **reserve averaging**: **90 per cent of CRR on a daily basis** retained; the **SDF** to be operationalised early; **communication**: **Money Market Operations** release to show **daily flow and stock impact**, and a **fortnightly durable liquidity assessment**.

**Revised framework in practice:** with **WACR** as the single target the **one-sided liquidity target was removed**; the **daily fixed rate repo and the 14-day term repos were withdrawn**; a **14-day term repo/reverse repo at a variable rate**, timed with the **CRR maintenance cycle**, became the **main liquidity tool** (with **fine-tuning operations**).

**Principles:** deficit or surplus is a **design choice**; **fixed rate operations** when **normal**, **variable rate** for **unanticipated** conditions; **banks should prefer trading among themselves** (borrow in the inter-bank market at no more than the **central bank lending rate** and lend at no less than the **central bank borrowing rate**).

**OMO structure:** **government securities of 1 to 20/30 years** and **Treasury Bills (7, 14, 28, 91, 182, 365 days)**; **repos** inject, **reverse repos** absorb.

**Objectives:** **safety and liquidity** are the **twin objectives**; **return optimisation** is sought **within** those limits. The demand for reserves depends on the **exchange rate regime**, **openness**, the **size of the external sector** and **market depth**.

**Why hold reserves:** they show **comfort in meeting international obligations (import payments)** and give a **cushion against external shocks** and **volatile capital flows**. The **transactions motive** is largely met by a **market-determined exchange rate**, but in **transition** reserves **smooth adjustment** and give **additional comfort**.

**Legal framework:** the **RBI Act, 1934** (**Sections 17(6A), 17(12), 17(12A), 17(13) and 33(6)**) allows investment in **deposits with other central banks and the BIS**, **deposits with commercial banks overseas**, **sovereign or sovereign-guaranteed debt with residual maturity up to 10 years**, and other instruments approved by the **Central Board**. Currency composition and investment policy are set **in consultation with the Government**.

**Risks and controls:**

| Risk | Management |
| --- | --- |
| **Credit** | **Highly rated sovereigns, central banks, supranationals**; deposits with **central banks, the BIS, commercial banks**; **counterparty selection guidelines** and **continuous limit monitoring** |
| **Market** | **Currency, interest rate and gold price** risk; gains and losses booked in the **Currency and Gold Revaluation Account (CGRA)**; **dated securities** valued at **market prices weekly and monthly** with changes going to the **Investment Revaluation Account (IRA)** as a **buffer** |
| **Currency** | Long-term **exposure decisions** reviewed regularly |
| **Interest rate** | **Benchmark duration** and **permitted deviation** |
| **Liquidity** | Portfolio kept **highly liquid** (Treasury securities can be sold in size; **fixed deposits** and **supranational** paper are less liquid); the portion convertible into cash at **short notice** is monitored |

old:
**Adequacy indicators (December 2021):** **import cover** fell to **13.1 months** (from **14.6** in September 2021); **short-term debt (original maturity) to reserves** rose from **16.5 to 18.1 per cent**; **volatile capital flows to reserves** rose from **64.1 to 65.0 per cent**. Reserve assets are about **two thirds of India's international financial assets**.

**Variation:** over **2021-22** the rise in **foreign-owned assets in India (USD 65.8 billion)** exceeded the rise in **overseas assets of residents (USD 61.1 billion)**, so **net claims of non-residents rose by USD 4.6 billion**; **exchange rate changes** (the **rupee depreciated about 2 per cent** in the quarter) affect **liabilities valued in US dollars**.

**Gold:** at **end-March 2022** the Reserve Bank held **760.42 tonnes** (**453.52 tonnes abroad** with the **Bank of England and the BIS**, **295.82 tonnes domestic**); the **gold share of reserves** rose from about **5.88 to 7.01 per cent**.

**Deployment of FCA (March 2022):** about **67 per cent in securities**, **26 per cent in deposits with other central banks and the BIS** and **7 per cent in deposits with commercial banks overseas**.

**Other items:** the IMF **Financial Transaction Plan** (purchases and repurchases), **New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB)** (India's commitment doubled from **1 January 2021**) and the **Note Purchase Agreement**; **SAARC swap arrangements** (Bhutan, Maldives, Sri Lanka); the Reserve Bank may invest up to **USD 5 billion** in bonds of the **India Infrastructure Finance Company (UK)**.

**Summing up:** reserves are a **comfort level** and **insulation** from external shocks, meet **precautionary** needs and build **confidence**; the Reserve Bank sold dollars to stabilise the rupee after **February 2022**.

**Early banking (Box 13.1):** the **East India Company** set up the **Bank of Bombay (1720)**; **Warren Hastings** floated the **General Bank of Bengal and Bihar (1773)**; the **General Bank of India (1786)**. The **Presidency Banks**: **Bank of Calcutta (1806)** → **Bank of Bengal (1809)**, **Bank of Bombay (1840)**, **Bank of Madras (1843)**; the **Paper Currency Act, 1861** ended their note issue; the **Presidency Banks Act 1876** put them under one law; the **Imperial Bank of India (1921)** merged them; after the **All India Rural Credit Survey** the **SBI Act (May 1955)** created the **State Bank of India (1 July 1955)**; the **1959 Subsidiary Banks Act** added associates, and the **associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank merged with SBI from 1 April 2017**.

**Early law:** banking was governed by the **Companies Acts** (**1850**, **1857**, **1913**); **limited liability** for banks came later. The **1913 crisis** exposed **low cash ratios** and **large unsecured advances to directors**; the **Indian Central Banking Enquiry Committee (1929-31)** urged a **special Bank Act**; interim measures were the **Banking Companies (Inspection) Ordinance and (Restriction of Branches) Act, 1946**; the **Banking Companies Act, 1949** (later the **Banking Regulation Act, 1966**) followed; the **Department of Banking Operations** of the Reserve Bank (organised **August 1945**) administered it.

**Monetary policy and supervision in India:** financial stability is intertwined with **macroeconomic stability**; **banking distress and currency crises are linked**; banks are the **main vehicle of monetary policy signals**. Supervision gives the Reserve Bank **information** on how its policy affects banks and helps **calibrated tools**. Example: in **December 2004** the **risk weight on housing loans rose from 50 to 75 per cent** and on **consumer credit from 100 to 125 per cent**; in **July 2005** capital market and commercial real estate exposures rose **from 100 to 125 per cent**. The courseware concludes that in India monetary policy and supervision are **complementary rather than conflicting**.

**Initial years (1950-1969):** many banks failed before 1950; the Reserve Bank's inspection powers began in **1940**, widened by the **Banking Companies (Inspection) Ordinance, 1946** (no prior consent of the bank needed); the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** requires the Reserve Bank, **before granting a licence**, to be satisfied that the company can **pay depositors in full**. Inspection shifted from a **quantitative check of paid-up capital and reserves** to a **qualitative appraisal of financial position, management and methods**; **systematic periodical inspections of all banks started in March 1950**. The **Act was amended in January 1957** (including **refinance** provisions). After the **Palai Central Bank and Laxmi Commercial Bank** collapse (**1960**), the Reserve Bank gained powers for **amalgamation** and **speedy de-licensing**, strengthened inspection (**1961**), looked at **capital adequacy norms** and began **deposit insurance**. The 1960-68 thrust: **soundness**, **consolidation**, **protection of small depositors** (compulsory amalgamations and liquidations), **correcting lopsided branch distribution** by **branch licensing**, and **social control (1967)** over credit deployment.

**Nationalisation and consolidation (1969-91):** **14 banks nationalised on 19 July 1969**; boards constituted on **18 July 1970**; the **National Credit Council** and the **Lead Bank Scheme (December 1969)**; a **branch expansion plan for 1972-74**; **Annual Appraisal** inspection added in **1977-78**; **6 more banks nationalised in 1980**; the target of **40 per cent priority sector advances by 1985**; the **Annual Financial Review from January 1985**; a **Working Group on inspection (December 1981)**.

**1990s reforms:** efficiency and profitability had fallen (directed credit, over-staffing, weak technology), so the **Narasimham Committee (1991)** led to **interest rate deregulation**, **lower CRR and SLR**, **operational autonomy** and prudential norms; **guidelines for entry of private banks in 1993**.

**Supervisory tools:** the Reserve Bank follows **Basel principles**: **capital adequacy**, **asset classification**, **income recognition**, **market valuation of assets** and **recovery of NPAs**, using **on-site** and **off-site** supervision. **Micro-prudential indicators** by **CAMELS** category (**capital ratio; sectoral concentration, foreign currency lending, NPAs, connected lending; expense ratios; ROA and ROE; loan-to-deposit ratio and inter-bank rate spreads; risk management and audit systems; foreign exchange, interest rate, equity and commodity price sensitivity; market-based indicators**) aggregate into the **AMPI**; they are combined with **macroeconomic indicators** and **stress tests** to form **macro-prudential indicators**.

**Returns:** **1999 ALM guidelines** introduced the **Statement of Structural Liquidity** (fortnightly: **domestic, foreign, combined Indian operations, overseas, consolidated**) and **interest rate sensitivity** (earnings perspective by **Traditional Gap Analysis, TGA**). **November 2012** revisions aligned with **Basel III**: **Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR)** and **Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR)** returns (**BLR 1 to 5**), and **Duration Gap Analysis (DGA)** (modified duration gap, by currency, monthly) **in addition to** TGA.

**Risk management (October 1999 guidelines):** **four risks** (**market, credit, legal, operational**) plus **systemic risk**; the **Board** sets risk parameters; implementation by a **Risk Management Committee**; a high-level **Credit Policy Committee (CPC)** and an independent **Credit Risk Management Department**; the **ALCO** and CPC integrate credit and market risk. **Credit risk** tools: Board-approved **loan policy**, **delegation of powers**, exposure limits (**single borrower, group, industry, region, sector**), **rating systems**, **loan review mechanism** and **rigorous evaluation of off-balance sheet and inter-bank/country exposures**. **Market risk** tools: **duration, EaR, VaR, simulation, RAROC**. **Interest rate risk:** **gap limits**, **VaR/duration/simulation** and **stress tests**; **currency risk**: **gap limits** with RBI approval and **VaR on forwards**; **operational risk**: proper **measurement and control systems**.

**Regulatory approaches to market risk:** **building block (BBA, as in the 1988 Basel market risk standards)**, **internal models (IMA)** and **pre-commitment (PCA)**.

**2020-21 goals:** refine the **regulatory framework**, a paper on **capital adequacy in UCBs**, a **Supervisory Action Framework (SAF)** for **StCBs and DCCBs** (**NABARD is their supervisor**), and faster resolution of **weak UCBs under All-Inclusive Directions (AID)**. Consolidation is hindered because UCBs are **community or region based**; an **expert committee** (February 2021) studied it.

**Other measures:** **system-based asset classification** (UCBs with assets of **Rs 2,000 crore or more**: from **30 June 2021**; **Rs 1,000-2,000 crore and Level III/IV in cyber security self-assessment**: from **30 September 2021**); **all co-operative banks eligible** for the MSME **Interest Subvention Scheme 2018** (from **3 March 2020**); **ban on director-related loans** (**5 February 2021**); the **umbrella organisation (UO)** for UCBs, **National Urban Co-operative Finance and Development Corporation Ltd (incorporated 18 April 2020)**, to be an **NBFC**.

**Four-tier framework (released 19 July 2022; notified 1 December 2022):**

| Tier | UCBs |
| --- | --- |
| **Tier 1** | **All unit UCBs and salary earners' UCBs**, and others with **deposits up to Rs 100 crore** |
| **Tier 2** | Deposits **above Rs 100 crore up to Rs 1,000 crore** |
| **Tier 3** | **Above Rs 1,000 crore up to Rs 10,000 crore** |
| **Tier 4** | **Above Rs 10,000 crore** |

Deposits are measured on the **audited balance sheet of 31 March** of the previous year; a bank moving up a tier gets a **glide path of up to three years**.

**Net worth:** **Rs 2 crore** for **Tier 1 UCBs in a single district**, **Rs 5 crore** for all others; shortfalls to reach **50 per cent by 31 March 2026** and **full by 31 March 2028**.

**CRAR:** **9 per cent** for **Tier 1**, **12 per cent** for **Tiers 2 to 4** (glide: **10 per cent by March 2024, 11 per cent by March 2025, 12 per cent by March 2026**).

**Financially Sound and Well Managed (FSWM) criteria:** (a) **CRAR at least 1 percentage point above the applicable minimum**; (b) **net NPA not above 3 per cent**; (c) **net profit in at least three of the preceding four years** and **no net loss in the last year**; (d) **no CRR/SLR default** in the previous year; (e) **sound internal control with at least two professional directors**; (f) **Core Banking Solution fully implemented**; (g) **no monetary penalty in the last two years**.
